global.headline: US RESUMES STRIKES ACROSS SOUTHERN IRAN OVER HORMUZ MINES; IRAN SAYS FOUR DIED AT A WEDDING AND FIRES BACK
summary: US Central Command began striking Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targets inside Iran at noon Eastern time on Tuesday, the largest American action since the strike pause that had held through most of August. CENTCOM said the strikes answered recent IRGC attempts to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and to attack American service members in the region, but did not say precisely what it was trying to destroy. Iranian state-linked outlets reported explosions across the south — Bandar Abbas, Qeshm, Sirik, Konarak and Chabahar. Trump said the strikes were retaliation for Iran's attempt to lay fresh sea mines in the strait and for the eight ballistic missiles fired at a US base in Jordan on Monday.

Iranian state media said four people were killed and dozens injured when a strike hit a house in southern Iran where a wedding was being held, among them a child. The claim has not been independently verified and CENTCOM has not addressed it. The IRGC, in a statement carried by the state broadcaster, said 'several of our fighters and compatriots' were killed and wounded. Iranian news agencies said retaliatory missile and drone attacks on US targets had begun within hours, though no independent confirmation of damage had emerged by the close of this window.

The trigger sits inside an unresolved dispute over whether the strait is mined at all. On Monday Iranian state TV, citing the IRGC, said a supertanker had caught fire and been brought to a halt after striking two naval mines in the southern strait, warning that other vessels breaking its passage rules would 'face the same fate'; the Guards named neither the ship nor its crew. CENTCOM publicly called the report false and described it as a disinformation campaign meant to intimidate commercial shipping. Both claims stand against Trump's own 28 August declaration that the strait had been fully demined, posted as 'MISSION ACCOMPLISHED 2026'.

Brent crude rose 0.87% to about US$91.28 a barrel on Tuesday, extending Monday's gain and holding above US$90 for a second session. Trump has again extended his threats to Kharg Island, the terminal handling the bulk of Iran's crude exports, which has been floated as a target since July and has still never been struck.
global.geopolitical: The month in which this war was fought with sanctions rather than munitions is over, and the return to shooting has happened in both directions within seventy-two hours. What makes this round harder to de-escalate than July's is that the two sides no longer agree on the underlying facts: Washington says Iran was preparing to lay mines and that the tanker report is fabricated, Tehran says a mined tanker is proof its rules must be obeyed, and Trump's own demining declaration a week ago now cuts against his administration's stated reason for striking. When the casus belli is contested, mediators have nothing to arbitrate. Oman's phased corridor framework and Qatar's shuttle diplomacy were built for a dispute about terms; this is a dispute about what happened, and the Omani channel has no mechanism for verifying the strait independently of the two governments that are lying about it or being lied to.
global.socioeconomic: Oil above US$90 for a second straight session is now feeding directly into the bond story below: traders bidding up crude on Hormuz risk are simultaneously pricing central banks to raise rates against the resulting inflation, so the war premium is arriving in mortgage and business-loan costs on four continents rather than only at the pump. For shipping, the practical effect of an unverifiable mine claim is worse than a verified one. Owners and their insurers cannot price a hazard that one navy says is present and another says is invented, and the rational response to that uncertainty is to keep staying away — which is why traffic has stayed near a standstill even through the weeks when the guns were quiet. The reported wedding deaths, if confirmed, also mark the pattern that has driven Iranian domestic anger hardest through this war: strikes aimed at coastal military infrastructure that land in residential southern towns.

global.headline: RUSSIA TURNS ON UKRAINE'S RAILWAYS: SIX RAIL WORKERS KILLED IN A KYIV DEPOT STRIKE, AT LEAST 12 DEAD OVERNIGHT
summary: A Russian ballistic missile struck a locomotive depot in Kyiv overnight into Tuesday, killing six employees of Ukrzaliznytsia, the Ukrainian state railway, according to the company's chairman Oleksandr Pertsovsky. A workshop was destroyed outright and several fires broke out at the site. Traffic on two sections was suspended and later restored. The depot strike was part of a wider bombardment of Kyiv and the surrounding region that killed at least 12 people and wounded a dozen more, three of them children, on what Ukrainian officials described as the sixth consecutive night of drone attacks on the capital.

Ukrainian officials and analysts framed the attack as the opening of a deliberate campaign against the rail network rather than an incidental hit. Since the full-scale invasion began, 58 railway staff have been killed and at least 318 injured, but the concentration of strikes on depots, junctions and rolling stock is new. Ukrzaliznytsia is the country's civil backbone: it carries the majority of freight, evacuates civilians from front-line oblasts, and moves military supplies, and it has run largely uninterrupted for three and a half years.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Moscow is capitalising on a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors to sustain the tempo against Kyiv and lower morale in the capital. Ukraine is racing to field domestically produced interceptors to close the gap. The strikes also coincided with the start of the school year, with children in Kyiv beginning classes underground.
global.geopolitical: Targeting the railway is a choice about what kind of war this becomes. Rail is the one system that ties Ukraine's economy, its evacuation capacity and its logistics into a single network, and degrading it hits all three at once without requiring territorial gains. It also tests the interceptor arithmetic directly: Zelenskyy's complaint is not that Ukraine lacks air defences but that it lacks Patriot missiles to fire from them, a shortage that traces back to US production rates and to the licensing arrangement Kyiv has been negotiating in Washington since late July. Russia appears to have concluded that the shortfall is durable enough to plan a sustained infrastructure campaign around, which is a judgment about American industrial capacity as much as about Ukrainian defences.
global.socioeconomic: Ukraine's grain and steel exports, its humanitarian corridors and its labour mobility all move on Ukrzaliznytsia, and it has been the most reliable public service the state has provided through the war. Sustained damage to depots and rolling stock is slower to repair than damage to track — locomotives cannot be improvised — so the effects compound over months rather than resolving in days. The deaths are also a labour story: rail workers have now become a targeted occupational class, with 58 killed and 318 injured, and a railway that cannot recruit or retain crews degrades even where the physical network is intact.

global.headline: GERMANY PINS AN EXPLOSIVE DRONE AT LEIPZIG AIRPORT ON RUSSIAN INTELLIGENCE, SHUTTING THE BONN CONSULATE AND BERLIN'S RUSSIAN HOUSE
summary: Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told a joint Berlin news conference on Tuesday that a Russian intelligence service was behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport on 4 August. A drone carrying an explosive device was found on airport grounds near Ukrainian cargo aircraft; a second flying object struck a cargo plane, causing minor damage, and the aircraft later landed safely in Hannover. Dobrindt said the device bore 'the fingerprints of the Kremlin' and that investigators had proof the agents controlling the drone were acting on behalf of Russian state entities.

It is the first time Berlin has formally attributed an attempted attack on a German airport to Moscow. Leipzig/Halle is a principal hub for shipping military equipment to Ukraine. The government called the attack part of a systematic and concerted effort by Moscow to 'cause great damage' through a large number of hybrid attacks, and described the conduct as 'dangerous behaviour'.

Germany summoned the Russian ambassador and ordered the Russian consulate general in Bonn closed from 18 September, along with the Russian House cultural centre in Berlin. Berlin is separately pressing within the EU for additional sanctions and travel restrictions on Russian nationals and for more pressure on Russia's shadow fleet. Moscow accused Germany of manufacturing a pretext and warned it would respond to any measures. German police were separately investigating reported explosives at a power substation in Brandenburg the same day.
global.geopolitical: Formal attribution is the step that converts a hybrid attack from a policing matter into a state-to-state one, and Germany has now taken it over an incident on NATO territory involving explosives and an airport. That is a materially higher rung than the arson, cable-cutting and drone-sighting incidents European governments have absorbed since 2024 without naming Moscow outright, and it commits Berlin to a response ladder it has so far avoided climbing. Closing a consulate and a cultural centre is the conventional first rung and invites a symmetrical Russian expulsion; the harder question is what Germany does when the next one happens, because the logic of attribution is that unanswered attacks invite repetition. Alliance-wide, an explosive device placed beside aircraft carrying military aid to Ukraine sits uncomfortably close to the threshold at which allies start debating Article 4 consultations.
global.socioeconomic: The commercial exposure runs through civil aviation. Leipzig/Halle is one of Europe's largest cargo hubs, home to DHL's main European operation, and drone incidents have already shown they can halt traffic at German airports for hours at a time regardless of whether anything detonates. Insurers and freight operators now have to price the possibility that a hub can be closed at will by a device costing a few thousand euros, which is a far cheaper form of disruption than anything sanctions can impose in return. Berlin's parallel push for shadow-fleet measures is the reciprocal lever: the fleet is how Russian crude reaches buyers above the price cap, and restricting it is one of the few responses that costs Moscow more than it costs Germany.

global.headline: GOVERNMENT BOND YIELDS HIT MULTI-DECADE HIGHS WORLDWIDE, THREATENING TO SQUEEZE BORROWERS FROM MORTGAGES TO BUSINESS LOANS
summary: A global bond sell-off deepened sharply on Tuesday, pushing long-term government borrowing costs to their highest levels in decades. UK 30-year gilt yields leapt as much as 0.12 percentage points to touch 5.9%, a level not seen since the late 1990s. Japan's 10-year yield reached 3%, its highest since 1996. Germany's 10-year yield hit its highest since 2011 and France's its highest since 2008.

Investors are betting that the Federal Reserve and other central banks will step up the pace of interest-rate rises this month, with the escalation in the Middle East pushing oil higher and reviving inflation fears. The sell-off also reflects longer-standing anxiety about government debt levels and deficits: bond markets are demanding more compensation to hold long-dated paper from governments issuing a great deal of it.

The pressure is political as well as financial. Rising borrowing costs add to the constraints on UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham ahead of next month's budget, and on Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who has faced repeated questions about how she intends to fund her economic stimulus plans. The effects extend well beyond government finances to mortgages, business loans and other credit priced off long-term yields.

The move landed a day after the head of the Financial Stability Board, Andrew Bailey, warned G20 finance ministers that ballooning government and private-sector debt, alongside stretched valuations at AI companies and the risk of AI-enabled cyberattacks, represent the principal threats to financial stability.
global.geopolitical: Long-dated yields are the market's running assessment of whether governments can keep spending at the pace their politics require, and the answer arriving simultaneously in London, Tokyo, Berlin and Paris is that they cannot do so cheaply. That constrains the two things Western governments are currently trying to do at once: rearm and cushion households against energy prices. Both are financed by issuing more long-dated debt into a market that is charging more for it, and the Iran war is what connects them — the same escalation that raises the case for defence spending is the escalation raising oil and therefore the inflation premium in the yield. Japan crossing 3% is the structurally largest event here, because three decades of near-zero Japanese yields have anchored the global cost of capital by pushing Japanese savings abroad; that flow reverses as domestic paper starts paying.
global.socioeconomic: This is the point at which a war premium stops being an abstraction on a commodity screen and becomes a household expense. Mortgage rates in the UK, corporate borrowing in the euro area and consumer credit generally reprice off exactly these benchmarks, with a lag of weeks to months, so the squeeze arriving now was set in motion by the escalation of the past fortnight. Governments face the same arithmetic from the other side: every percentage point on long-term yields consumes budget room that would otherwise fund services, which is why Burnham's budget and Takaichi's stimulus are both suddenly harder to write. For Singapore, whose mortgage market prices largely off SORA rather than these benchmarks directly, the transmission is indirect but real, running through global funding costs and the Singapore Government Securities curve.

global.headline: FRANCE VOTES A PER-GARMENT LEVY ON ULTRA-FAST FASHION AS SHEIN LISTS IN HONG KONG AT A QUARTER OF ITS FORMER VALUE
summary: The French Senate on Tuesday adopted a bill regulating ultra-fast fashion by 337 votes to one, having passed the National Assembly in March 2024. It imposes an escalating per-item levy and bans advertising of the products it covers. The 2026 rates start at 50 euro cents on a pair of underwear (about S$0.75), rising to €2 on a T-shirt (about S$2.95), €9 on jeans (about S$13.30) and €12 on a jacket (about S$17.70), scaling toward as much as €19.50 per item by 2030 (about S$28.80) — capped at 50% of the product's pre-tax price.

A garment counts as ultra-fast fashion on two criteria: the volume of clothing the seller places on the market, and the cost of repairing a garment relative to its purchase price. The scale is calibrated to how each product scores on both. The design deliberately catches Shein, Temu and AliExpress while leaving conventional high-street chains such as H&M and Zara outside its scope, and follows a June law aimed at disposable fashion's environmental toll.

The vote landed on the same day Shein finally reached a public market. Its Hong Kong debut valued the China-founded company at about US$26 billion (roughly S$33 billion), around a quarter of the roughly US$100 billion (about S$127 billion) it once commanded, and shares slid by as much as 10% on the first day of trading. The listing followed years of failed attempts to float in New York and then London.
global.geopolitical: France has done what the EU has spent two years declining to do, and the mechanism matters more than the money: by defining ultra-fast fashion through volume and repairability rather than by naming companies or countries of origin, Paris has built a levy that is difficult to challenge as discriminatory while landing almost entirely on Chinese-founded platforms. That is a template other member states can copy without waiting for Brussels, and it will be read in Beijing alongside the EU's parcel-import reforms as a coordinated squeeze on the direct-to-consumer channel that has been China's most successful consumer-facing export of the decade. Shein's retreat from New York and London to Hong Kong completes the same picture from the other direction: a company that spent five years trying to become Western-listed has ended up firmly inside the Chinese capital-markets orbit.
global.socioeconomic: The levy is a straightforward transfer of cost onto low-income consumers, and it is meant to be — the theory is that a T-shirt priced to be thrown away is only cheap because its disposal and its emissions are paid for by someone else. Whether it changes behaviour depends on the price elasticity of a customer base that shops on Shein precisely because the alternatives are unaffordable; €2 on a T-shirt is a modest deterrent, €19.50 by 2030 is not. Shein's valuation tells the market's side of the story: at a quarter of its peak, the company is now priced as a business facing durable regulatory cost in its major Western markets rather than as an uncapped growth story, and the 10% first-day slide suggests even that mark was optimistic.

singapore.headline: MAS PROPOSES BINDING STABLECOIN LAW: FULL RESERVE BACKING, REDEMPTION AT PAR AND A BAN ON PAYING INTEREST
summary: The Monetary Authority of Singapore published a consultation paper on 1 September setting out draft amendments to the Payment Services Act 2019 to give legal force to its single-currency stablecoin framework. The framework itself was finalised in 2023 but has never been binding; the amendments would define how an issuer qualifies as MAS-regulated and what it must do to keep that designation, covering reserve-asset management, capital adequacy, redemption at par value and disclosure.

Alongside implementing the 2023 design, MAS proposed new safeguards responding to how the market has moved since. Issuers seeking the regulated designation would be barred from paying interest on regulated stablecoins, would have to run stress tests, and would have to maintain recovery plans and an orderly wind-down plan should the business run into financial or operational trouble. The paper also addresses foreign issuers.
The consultation closes on 16 October 2026. MAS said it will consult separately on the accompanying subsidiary legislation at a later stage.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore is now legislating in the same window as the United States and the European Union, and converging on the same core requirements — full backing, redemption at par, no yield — which matters more for a jurisdiction whose pitch is regulatory credibility than being first would. The interest ban is the pointed choice: it forecloses the model in which a stablecoin competes with bank deposits by paying a return on its reserves, which is the design regulators everywhere blame for turning payment tokens into unstable quasi-banks. By writing that into statute rather than guidance, MAS makes the Singapore label portable — an issuer can tell a counterparty in Frankfurt or New York what standard it meets — and that portability is the actual product Singapore is selling here.
singapore.socioeconomic: The practical protection for users is the wind-down plan. Every stablecoin failure of the past four years has turned on the same question — who gets the reserves, in what order, and how fast — and answering it in advance, under statute, is worth more to a retail holder than any disclosure requirement. The interest ban has a cost attached: it removes the main reason a Singapore user would hold a regulated stablecoin rather than a deposit, so adoption will have to come from payments utility, particularly cross-border settlement, rather than yield. That is a deliberate narrowing, and it means the framework's success should be judged on remittance and trade-settlement volumes rather than on how many tokens are issued.

singapore.headline: PM WONG TRAVELS TO BANGKOK FOR THE FIRST SINGAPORE-THAILAND LEADERS' RETREAT IN ELEVEN YEARS
summary: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong makes a one-day visit to Thailand on Wednesday 2 September for the Singapore-Thailand Leaders' Retreat, hosted by Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul. It is the first retreat between the two leaders and the first of its kind since the last edition was held in Singapore in 2015, reviving a format that lapsed for eleven years.

The two leaders will review long-standing defence and economic cooperation and explore new collaboration in the green and digital economies, energy resilience, food security and combatting transnational crime. An agreement to deepen cooperation in social sector development is expected to be marked, followed by a joint press conference.
Mr Wong is accompanied by Mrs Wong and five other ministers. Mr Anutin hosts a private lunch and an official dinner.
singapore.geopolitical: Reviving a leaders' retreat after eleven dormant years is a deliberate signal, and the timing is about Thailand's neighbourhood as much as about Singapore's. Bangkok has spent 2026 managing a contested border with Cambodia, a fluid domestic political settlement and pressure to pick sides between Washington and Beijing on trade; a full-format retreat with Singapore gives Anutin a low-cost demonstration that ASEAN's most institutionally stable member takes his government seriously. For Singapore, the substantive item on the list is transnational crime, which for both countries now means the scam-compound economy operating out of the Myanmar border zones and moving money through regional banking systems. That is a problem neither can solve alone and one Singapore has an acute interest in, given how much of the proceeds transit its financial system.
singapore.socioeconomic: Energy resilience and food security are where this retreat could produce something concrete. Thailand is one of Singapore's principal sources of rice, poultry and eggs, and the ASEAN Power Grid work that Singapore has been assembling through cross-border electricity import deals depends on transmission corridors that run through Thai territory. Both agendas suit a Singapore that has been steadily diversifying supply lines since the pandemic and that now imports a small but growing share of its electricity. The green-economy strand also opens the possibility of carbon-credit arrangements under Article 6, which Singapore has been signing bilaterally to give its carbon-tax-paying companies offset options.

singapore.headline: EU HEALTH-SECURITY CHIEF VISITS ANG MO KIO MOSQUITO FACTORY TO STUDY WHETHER EUROPE CAN RUN ITS OWN PROJECT WOLBACHIA
summary: Florika Fink-Hooijer, director-general of the European Commission's Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority, visited Singapore's mosquito production facility in Ang Mo Kio on 1 September to assess whether European countries could adopt the Wolbachia approach to mosquito suppression. The visit follows the spread of tropical, mosquito-borne disease into a warming Europe.

Project Wolbachia, launched by the National Environment Agency in 2016, releases lab-grown male Aedes mosquitoes carrying the Wolbachia bacterium. Females that mate with them lay eggs that do not hatch, suppressing the population over successive generations. NEA reports mosquito populations at project sites down by 80 to 90 per cent and the risk of acquiring dengue lowered by more than 70 per cent.
The programme is on track for 50 per cent household coverage in Singapore during 2026, having scaled from small pilot estates over a decade.
singapore.geopolitical: This is the export of a public-health capability rather than a product, and it is the kind of soft power that is difficult to manufacture deliberately. Singapore built Project Wolbachia because it had no choice — a dense tropical city with year-round Aedes breeding and recurring dengue epidemics — and the result is a decade of operational data at city scale that simply does not exist anywhere in Europe. That the EU's health-emergency agency is sending its director-general to an Ang Mo Kio facility rather than commissioning its own trials reflects how much of the difficulty in this technique is industrial rather than scientific: rearing, sexing and releasing millions of male mosquitoes weekly, reliably, is a manufacturing problem Singapore has already solved.
singapore.socioeconomic: The reason Europe is asking now is climate: Aedes albopictus is established across the Mediterranean and moving north, and locally acquired dengue and chikungunya cases in France, Italy and Spain have risen from curiosities to annual occurrences. The alternative tools are insecticides, to which resistance is spreading, and genetically modified mosquito releases, which face far higher regulatory and public-acceptance barriers in the EU than a naturally occurring bacterium does. For Singapore the return is not commercial in any immediate sense, but the facility, the rearing know-how and the NEA's efficacy data become a reference standard others build to — and dengue control is one of the few areas where a small state's operational record outweighs any research budget.

singapore.headline: MET SERVICE WARNS HAZE COULD REACH SINGAPORE IN THE NEXT FORTNIGHT AS A MONTH OF DRY WEATHER PERSISTS
summary: The Meteorological Service Singapore said on 1 September that the dry conditions of the past month will continue through the first half of September, with fair and occasionally windy weather on most days, particularly in the first week. Sporadic showers are likely in the second week, but total rainfall for the fortnight is forecast to be below average over most of the island.

Dense smoke haze has been observed over southern and central Sumatra and parts of Kalimantan on most days since around 21 August. Under the prevailing south-easterly or south-westerly winds, Singapore may experience hazy conditions if those fires intensify.
Warm and humid nights are also expected to continue through the period.
singapore.geopolitical: Transboundary haze is the one recurring issue on which Singapore's diplomacy has the least leverage and the most at stake, and the machinery built for it — the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution, Singapore's own Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, the bilateral hotspot-monitoring arrangements — has never been tested against a bad year since 2019. Sustained dense smoke over Sumatra and Kalimantan since late August is the earliest signal in several years that this could be one. The practical constraint is unchanged: enforcement depends on Indonesian concession data that Jakarta has historically declined to share, so Singapore's options run to satellite monitoring, offers of firefighting assistance and quiet pressure rather than anything binding.
singapore.socioeconomic: A haze episode is a regressive event. Outdoor workers — construction, marine, landscaping, delivery — absorb the exposure that office workers do not, which is why MOM's heat-and-haze provisions and employer obligations on N95 supply matter more than air-purifier sales figures. Schools, childcare centres and eldercare facilities carry the next tranche of risk, and the health system sees it as a lagged rise in respiratory presentations rather than an immediate surge. The dryness itself has separate costs: below-average rainfall for a fortnight raises water-demand pressure at a time when NEWater and desalination already carry an energy cost that shows up in tariffs, and Singapore's Q3 electricity tariff is already at a record 34.78 cents per kWh including GST.

singapore.headline: UOL-CAPITALAND VENTURE BIDS A RECORD S$1,537 PSF PPR FOR A NEW UPPER CHANGI SITE, A SUBURBAN LAND BENCHMARK
summary: The tender for the New Upper Changi Road government land sales site closed on 1 September with four bids. A joint venture of UOL Group, CapitaLand Development and Singapore Land submitted the top bid of S$1.425 billion, or S$1,537 per square foot per plot ratio — a new benchmark for a pure residential GLS site in the Outside Central Region.

The bid was 13.8 per cent above the next highest, from City Developments and Hong Realty. The 99-year leasehold site, on the grounds of a former school in one of Bedok's established neighbourhoods, could yield roughly 1,010 units if the tender is accepted.
The result lands against a housing market in which HDB resale prices recorded their first quarterly decline since 2019 in the first quarter of this year.
singapore.geopolitical: Little direct international dimension, but the bid is a statement about where developers think Singapore residential demand is durable. Two of the country's largest listed developers were willing to pay a suburban record for a mass-market site at a moment when global long-term interest rates are hitting multi-decade highs, which is a bet that domestic housing demand is insulated from the funding-cost shock repricing credit elsewhere. It also reflects the structural feature of the Singapore market that foreign observers most often miss: with private residential land supply controlled almost entirely through the state's GLS programme, scarcity is a policy variable rather than a market outcome, and developers bid accordingly.
singapore.socioeconomic: A record land price flows directly into the eventual launch price, and at S$1,537 psf ppr the breakeven points toward the upper end of what has historically been called mass-market. That matters for the households this segment is meant to serve — HDB upgraders in the east — at exactly the moment resale prices have started softening and mortgage costs are rising with global yields. Roughly 1,010 additional units is real supply and works the other way, easing pressure over the three to four years until completion. The tension between those two effects, a record price now against a thousand units later, is the central trade-off in the government's supply-led approach to housing affordability.

word.definition: A political policy or animating spirit devoted to reversing the losses of an earlier defeat — territory, standing or prestige — and to avenging the humiliation of it; the pursuit of a settlement's undoing as a national purpose.
word.etymology: From French revanche, 'revenge', from Old French revenchier (re- 'back' + vengier 'to avenge', ultimately Latin vindicare, 'to claim, to avenge'). The -isme was attached in France after the Franco-Prussian War of 1870-71, when the loss of Alsace-Lorraine produced a political current — the revanchards — whose organising demand was that the provinces be won back. The word entered English in the 1920s and has since been applied to any state that treats a past defeat as an unfinished argument rather than a settled fact.
word.example: Germany's decision to name Russian intelligence as the author of the Leipzig drone attack, and Moscow's simultaneous turn against Ukraine's railways, were read in Berlin as two expressions of the same revanchism — a state that regards the post-1991 settlement as a wound rather than an outcome, and that is willing to place explosives beside cargo aircraft on NATO soil to say so.
